opening.headline: When you give a tool, but the model chooses the wrong tool, you learn how to find the cause in the tool's name, description, and response design and fix it.
body: Even though you hand your model multiple tools, she keeps picking the wrong tool for the same request. In this case, it's easy to blame the model, but the cause often lies in the tool definition.

In this class, we'll look at why tools should be contracts for agents rather than APIs for developers, conditions for good names and descriptions, token-saving response design, tool discovery when there are a lot of tools, and programmatic calls. At the end, we use examples to check which improvements are selected for each symptom and the order in which the tool is refined by repeating the evaluation.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the impact of tool name, description, and response design on selection accuracy
Allows you to determine where tool definitions need improvement

screens.title: I gave them tools, but they chose the wrong ones.
screens.lead: Read the scene where the model picks the wrong tool. It is a good idea to read this while thinking about whether it can be seen as a fault with the model or whether there are other causes.

visual.alt: A scene showing a user request, a list of tool names called by the model, and a list of erroneous results.
labels: Please tell me the recent payment history of customer 9182

paragraphs: A user asked: "Give me the latest payment history for customer 9182." In front of the model were tools with names such as `search_users`, `get_data`, and `query`, and the model called `get_data`. The result was thousands of customer lists that had nothing to do with the request.

What's more difficult is that even if you repeat the same request, you change tools and make wrong choices. When this phenomenon continues, it is easy to conclude that “the model is not working well.”

But look at the tool list again from a human perspective. Can you tell just by the name what `get_data` brings and how it differs from `query`? In fact, this name and description are all that the model sees. The cause may lie in the tool definition rather than the model.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If you were asked to choose a function created by a colleague based solely on its name, how accurately would you be able to choose it? The model's situation is not much different.

screens.outro: Let's hypothesize that the cause lies in the definition of the tool, and first recall your own experience.

screens.title: think about it
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever felt confused about what a function created by a teammate does just by looking at its name?
items.answer: If the name is ambiguous, people will have to open the code to find out. However, the model cannot open the code; it only sees the name and description. A tool that confuses people also confuses the model.

items.prompt: Have you ever crammed too much functionality into one API endpoint and found it difficult to write?
items.answer: If a tool does completely different things depending on its arguments, it is difficult to determine when to call it by which argument. Separating tools with mixed purposes makes it easier to make choices. Conversely, it is better to integrate tools with overlapping functions.

items.prompt: Have you ever found it difficult to find the information you need because the results are so long?
items.answer: The same goes for models. If your response is full of unnecessary fields, context is wasted and important information is buried. Tool responses should be designed to contain only information that helps the agent make decisions.

screens.outro: Starting from the fact that a tool that confuses people also confuses the model, let's look at what type of contract the tool is.

screens.title: Tools for Agents
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how a traditional function call differs from an agent call.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing the flow in which a function call is divided into one path and an agent call is divided into several branches.

states.label: function call
states.body: In traditional software, the same input is guaranteed to produce the same output, such as `getWeather("NYC")`. It is predictable because the caller knows exactly the function name and arguments. In this deterministic system, even if the name is somewhat ambiguous, a developer who reads the documentation can call it correctly.

states.label: agent call
states.body: Agents can take multiple paths to the same question. You can call a weather tool, respond with learned knowledge, or ask for a location. Because calls are non-deterministic, tools should be designed for agents rather than developer APIs. Tools that are easy for agents to handle are often intuitive for humans as well. A tool can be viewed as a contract between a deterministic system and a non-deterministic agent. Since the name and description of the tool correspond to the contract, the starting point of design is to write these two in a way that is easy for the agent to read. Choose a name based on the user's understanding, not convenience of implementation.

screens.outro: Let’s compare bad definitions and good definitions to see how the contents of a contract change in detail.

screens.title: Comparing bad and good definitions
screens.lead: Select a highlighted passage from the good definition below to see an explanation of what has changed from the bad definition.

visual.alt: A left-right comparison of a bad tool definition and a good tool definition with the same function.

data.text:
name: get_customer_payments
description: Returns one customer's payment history in reverse date order. Use when you know the customer number. Do not use when searching for a customer by name.. Returns up to 20 payments, most recent first.
input: customer_id (string, required)
input_examples: call with customer_id "9182"

Comparison: The bad definition had name as get_data, description as "get data", and argument as id..

marks.note: The name reveals the audience (customer) and actions (payments). A poorly defined get_data could not be distinguished from other tools because it was unclear what the data was from.

marks.span: Returns one customer's payment history in reverse date order
marks.note: What it does and how it returns is written in one sentence. Writing down the return form makes it easier for the model to determine whether the tool meets the request.

marks.span: Use when you know the customer number. Do not use when searching for a customer by name.
marks.note: I also wrote down when to use it and when not to use it. Reduce erroneous selections by clearly demarcating search_users with similar names.
Even the name of the character has meaning. I couldn't figure out what the bad definition id number was. The type and whether it is required or not are clearly small.
Giving an example call will help the model follow the correct argument shape. The example must fit the input_schema.

marks.span: The bad definition had name as get_data, description as "get data", and argument as id.
marks.note: Bad definition on the left card. The namespace method, which groups related tools with the same prefix and makes the boundaries clear, is also a way to increase selection accuracy.

screens.outro: Now that we've refined the name and description, let's look at how to design the response the tool returns.

screens.title: Token efficient tool response
screens.lead: The table shows common mistakes made when designing tool responses and directions for improvement. Read about the waste that occurs line by line.

data.caption: Tool Responsive Design: Inefficiencies and Improvements
rows: We waste context by including all unnecessary fields. It only lists values ​​such as internal identifiers and is not helpful in making decisions.
It first returns meaningful information that the agent can use to make decisions, such as a human-readable name. Leave only as many identifiers as are necessary for subsequent calls.
Returns all results at once. Broad hits bring thousands of items into context.
Allows you to control the response size with parameters such as page breaks, filters, and length limits. You can request only as many models as you need.
Only a short code with unknown cause is returned. The model makes the same call over and over again.
I write in a way that tells me what to do next. For example, if the argument format is incorrect, it will guide you to the correct format.
We do not log the number of calls and token consumption. Even if there is waste, you never know.
We gather the number of calls and token consumption as indicators to check for duplicate calls. You need indicators to see the effect of improvement.
data.notes: Because the responses go directly into the model's context, reducing responses not only benefits cost, but also improves judgment quality. There is also a way to set a parameter such as response_format that selects the level of detail of the response between concise and detailed. In Anthropic's example, the concise response used about one-third of the tokens. Even if there are no results or failure, please return it with a meaningful sentence. For example, if you can't find a customer, don't just return an empty list. Instead, return a statement saying it couldn't be found and providing instructions for another method, so the model can decide its next action. Instead of making improvements all at once, change items one by one and compare indicators. You can see which changes worked.

screens.outro: Let's continue to see what to do if the tools themselves become too numerous even after you've refined the answer.

screens.title: Tool discovery and programmatic invocation
screens.lead: When you select an item, the text expands. Open and check each of the two means when you have more tools.

items.title: Problem: Tool definition eats context
items.body: Uploading all of the tool definitions is burdensome. In the example in the article, a configuration that connects GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana, and Splunk spends about 55k tokens just on definitions before it even starts working. The document also explains that Claude's tool selection accuracy decreases when there are more than 30 to 50 tools available. Having more tools doesn't mean the model makes better choices. As the number of connected servers increases, this burden quickly increases.

items.title: Tool Search
items.body: Tool search finds and retrieves only the tools needed at the time of request, and the documentation explains that it typically retrieves 3 to 5 tools per request and reduces definition tokens by over 85 percent. Rather than having the entire list on hand at all times, the model retrieves only the definitions it needs at the moment it is needed. Selection accuracy can be maintained as the number of tokens occupied by definitions is reduced and the number of candidates is reduced.

items.title: programmatic call
items.body: Programmatic calls are when your code calls a tool multiple times within a code execution container, filters the results, and returns them to the model. For example, if you handle a recurring query to check budgets for 20 employees in one script, there are fewer round trips to the model and fewer tokens. This is useful when the model does not need to read all intermediate results.

items.title: Criteria for choosing between two methods
items.body: If the number of tools is an issue, consider tool discovery. If calling the same tool dozens of times over and over again is an issue, consider programmatic calls. The two methods have different problems to solve, so check the symptoms first before choosing.

screens.outro: Now that you know the three means of improvement, I will explain which treatment to choose for each symptom.

screens.title: Commentary: Improved integration, separation, and explanation when selection errors increase
screens.lead: The instructor goes through the symptoms one by one and determines which improvement to choose. Select the right arrow to check symptoms and prescriptions in turn.

visual.alt: A diagram in the form of a judgment table where prescriptions are linked to each symptom.
labels: Switching between two tools with similar names
Improve description or merge into one
One tool does completely different things depending on its arguments
As the number of tools increases, accuracy decreases.
Invoking the same tool dozens of times in one task
Programmatic call or batch processing tool

steps.title: First, collect usage records
steps.body: For any symptom, we collect actual usage records and look at call patterns before prescribing a prescription. Looking at which request, which tool was chosen, and what the results were, can provide clues as to whether the cause is a description or structure problem. If you fix it by guessing, you may end up fixing something in the wrong place. Also check if the same request goes to the same tool every time or if it fluctuates.

steps.title: Symptom A: Jumping between similar tools
steps.body: If you are going back and forth between two tools with similar names, it means that the boundaries between the two tools are blurry. The prescription is to improve explanations or consolidate them into one. If there is at least enough overlap in the descriptions of when to use and when not to use, it is better to combine them into one.

steps.title: Symptom B: Doing completely different things depending on the factor
steps.body: If a tool does completely different things depending on its arguments, its purpose is mixed. The model gets confused about which combination of factors does what. The prescription is to separate tools by purpose.

steps.title: Symptom C: As the number of tools increases, accuracy decreases.
steps.body: As you continue to add tools, there will be too many candidates and accuracy will decrease. At this point, no matter how much you refine the name and description, there are limits. The prescription is to use search tools to retrieve only what you need.

steps.title: Symptom D: Calling the same tool dozens of times per task
steps.body: For example, if you look up the information of dozens of employees one by one, dozens of round trips will occur. The prescription is to leave repetitive queries to code with programmatic calls, or to create a batch processing tool that handles multiple queries at once.

steps.title: When applied to the first case,
steps.body: The first get_data case is closer to symptom A. The name was vague and the description was poor, so it had no boundaries with similar tools. Therefore, the first prescription is to specify the name and write in the description the point of use and the form of return. If you're still confused about search_users, consider integrating the two tools into one.

screens.outro: After applying the prescription, you should check its effectiveness. Let’s look at the order of creating evaluation and iterative improvement.

screens.title: Commentary: The sequence for creating assessments and iteratively improving tools
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of creating and refining tools step by step. Selecting the right arrow adds a step and closes the loop.

visual.alt: A tool improvement cycle with five steps leading through circular arrows.
labels: Run agent in loop and record metrics
Read your conversation history to find points of confusion
Accuracy, number of calls, tokens, errors

steps.title: 1. Create a draft and write it yourself
steps.body: Create a draft of the tool and try using it yourself. When you call a tool, the first thing you notice is that the name and arguments are awkward. Your draft doesn't have to be perfect; it just needs to be good enough to be evaluated. It is quicker to turn it around first and then refine it.

steps.title: 2. Collect evaluation items from actual work
steps.body: Gather tasks that require multiple steps taken from real jobs into assessment items. Tasks that require the use of multiple tools in succession are more likely to reveal selection errors than simple one-time requests.

steps.title: 3. Run and record through agent loop
steps.body: It loops through the agent and records accuracy, number of calls, tokens, and errors. In addition to accuracy, looking at call count and tokens together can help you find duplicate calls or waste.

steps.title: 4. Read conversation logs
steps.body: Don't just look at metrics, read conversation transcripts directly to find where the model got confused. The records reveal which tool was selected, why it was selected, and what factor caused the blockage. Here we find the reason that numbers cannot tell.

steps.title: 5. Fix it and run it again
steps.body: Fix the description and schema and run the evaluation again. Check if your metrics are improving, and if not, go back to your conversation history. If you change several places at once, it will be difficult to distinguish the effect, so change them one at a time. As this cycle closes, the tool becomes increasingly tailored to the agent. Increase the number of evaluation items over time, and be sure to add any newly discovered failures to prevent the same problem from recurring.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: If people are confused, the model is also confused.
screens.lead: Let's go back to our initial get_data example and tie the design principles of this lesson together.

paragraphs: The initial poor choice was not due to a lack of model capabilities, but was due to the ambiguity of the tool definition. Since the model selects a tool based solely on its name and description, the name, description, and parameter names must be unambiguous. Your choice will be more accurate if you write in the description when to use it and when not to use it and what it returns.

Because tools are contracts between a deterministic system and a non-deterministic agent, they must be designed differently than human APIs. Responses are pared down to only contain information that is meaningful to the agent and save tokens. Integrate tools with overlapping functions, and separate tools with mixed purposes.

If you have many tools, tool search retrieves only what you need, and bundles multiple repeated calls into programmatic calls. And what to fix is ​​decided not by guessing but by reading evaluations and conversation records. The cycle of fixing and reworking is a core habit of tool design.

The inspection you can do today is simple. Collect the names and descriptions of the tools you have, and see if a colleague who is meeting you for the first time can tell their purpose. If you have a tool that doesn't differentiate, that's the first candidate for improvement. It is recommended that you repeat this check whenever you add a new tool.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: If you're shaky on your choice, check the names, descriptions, responses, and number of tools in that order before blaming the model. The basis for inspection is always actual usage records.

glossary.def: Plaintext description that the model reads when selecting a tool. Write down when you spend and what you return.
This is a method of distinguishing functional areas by adding a prefix to the tool name.
This is a function that finds and loads only the necessary tools among numerous tools.
The code calls the tool multiple times, filters the results, and returns them to the model.
This is a property that saves context by reducing tool responses to only necessary information.

misconceptions.myth: The more tools you have, the better the model you choose.
misconceptions.fact: If you have more than 30 to 50 tools, selection accuracy may decrease. When dealing with a lot of tools, you can use tool search to retrieve only what you need.

misconceptions.myth: The more detailed the tool response, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Unnecessary fields waste context and bury important information. First, return meaningful information that will be used in the agent’s judgment.

misconceptions.myth: If the model chooses the wrong tool, it is a model problem.
misconceptions.fact: Ambiguous names and poor descriptions are often the culprits. A tool that confuses people just by looking at its name also confuses the model.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Since the model selects a tool based solely on its name and description, use unambiguous names, descriptions, and parameter names.
Tools are designed differently than human APIs because they are a contract between a deterministic system and a non-deterministic agent.
Responses are pared down to only contain information that is meaningful to the agent and save tokens.
Integrate tools with overlapping functions, and separate tools with mixed purposes.
If you have a lot of tools, tool search will load only what you need, or if you want to bundle multiple calls into code, use programmatic calls.
